headline: Pilbara Minerals crashes 8% as Citi cuts lithium targets — but GTA VI hype lifts Take-Two to a fresh high, and last night's US market rally keeps the broader portfolio steady.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a rough session, dropping 8% to close at $2.85. The catalyst was Citi cutting price targets on lithium miners today, flagging that the market is heading for a surplus — meaning more lithium is being produced than the world currently needs. That's bad news for Pilbara's earnings outlook, and the stock is now down nearly 58% from what you paid. The long-term electric vehicle story is intact, but oversupply is a real headwind right now.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped 2.26% in last night's session to US$521.13. No single dramatic catalyst, but post-earnings analysis suggests the market is scrutinising Microsoft's heavy AI infrastructure spending versus near-term revenue returns from those investments. Google's strong night may have also pulled some attention away. Despite the dip, Microsoft is still up over 17% from your cost base — the long-term AI and cloud story remains solid.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two jumped nearly 3% last night to US$231.31, continuing the GTA VI hype wave. Xbox confirmed GTA VI will launch on Xbox Cloud Gaming on November 19, opening up the game to millions of subscribers who don't own the console outright. That's a meaningful expansion of the potential player base and bodes well for day-one sales momentum.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google rose 2% last night to US$290.63. Search revenue continues to show solid growth and the market responded positively to analysis highlighting Google's earnings trajectory. Despite the good night, your small position is still slightly underwater overall at -5.5% — but the long-term fundamentals look fine.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS added 1.06% today to close at $545.79, tracking last night's strong US market session where the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both rallied. Your position is now up 5.8% overall — a steady performer doing exactly what it's supposed to.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI edged up 0.76% today to $15.95, getting a small lift from the broader AI optimism in markets. It's still carrying a -15.5% loss overall, largely from the sector's earlier pullback this year. The Motley Fool flagged GXAI as one of the best AI ETFs to hold for 2026, so the long-term case hasn't changed.

movers.name: DHHF.AX
movers.note: DHHF quietly ticked up 0.45% today to $42.55 — a small but positive move reflecting the broadly steady ASX session. This diversified ETF is doing its job: smoothing out the bumps from individual stock volatility elsewhere in your portfolio.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG added 0.36% today to close at $77.52. It's essentially flat on the year at just +0.34% total return, but that reflects the mixed global market conditions of 2026. As a diversified high-growth fund, it's meant for the long haul — no concerns here.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was virtually unchanged today, closing at $91.66. Emerging markets have been under pressure from a weaker AUD and global risk-off sentiment tied to the Iran conflict. Down 3% overall, but this is a long-term diversifier — sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Citi cuts targets — but hold for the long term
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped 8% today to $2.85 after Citi slashed lithium miner price targets, warning the market is moving into surplus territory. You're down 57.7% on this position — painful, but selling now locks in that loss. The EV transition story hasn't collapsed; it's just taking longer than expected. If you can stomach the volatility, holding gives you exposure to any lithium price recovery. Only consider selling if you need the capital or no longer believe in the EV thesis.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA VI launch week approaching — good time to hold
watch_today.detail: Take-Two rose ~3% last night and GTA VI hits Xbox Cloud Gaming on November 19 — just days away. This is the moment TTWO has been building toward for years. Your position is up 7.2% overall and momentum is with the stock heading into the biggest game launch in history. No reason to sell ahead of a potential further catalyst.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Short-term dip, long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: Microsoft dropped 2.26% last night — the market is questioning whether its massive AI spending will pay off quickly enough. But you're still up 17.6% on your position and Microsoft's Azure cloud and Copilot AI products are genuinely world-class. A single bad night doesn't change the thesis. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: Iran conflict: watch oil prices this week
watch_today.detail: The US-Iran war is ongoing and talks on a ceasefire are making little progress. Iran has warned of domestic gas shortages this winter, and the US is tightening a blockade with limited support from regional neighbours. Oil (WTI) is sitting at US$86.92 — elevated but stable for now. Any escalation around the Strait of Hormuz (a critical shipping chokepoint) could spike oil and hit global markets. Worth watching through the week.

watch_today.title: AUD slipping — adds pressure on import costs and RBA
watch_today.detail: The Aussie dollar fell 0.62% last night to US$0.6827. The AFR flagged today that a weak AUD is starting to complicate the RBA's (Reserve Bank of Australia's) fight against inflation — a weaker dollar makes imported goods more expensive, which can push prices up just as the RBA is trying to bring them down. This matters for your US-listed holdings too: a weaker AUD boosts the AUD value of GOOG, MSFT, and TTWO when you eventually convert back.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF nudging higher — hold for the long run
watch_today.detail: GXAI ticked up 0.76% today and was highlighted by Motley Fool as one of the best AI ETFs for 2026. You're still down 15.5% overall, but AI regulation news (both globally and in Australia) is a watch point — tighter rules could weigh on the sector short-term. Long-term, the AI growth story is real. Hold.

world.summary: The US-Iran war continues to dominate global news, with no ceasefire in sight and oil markets on edge. Meanwhile, US domestic politics is in turmoil after midterm results, and global economic conditions are holding firm but getting harder.

stories.title: US-Iran War: No progress on talks, blockade tightening
stories.why_it_matters: The 2026 US-Iran war is grinding on with no end in sight. Iran is now warning its own citizens of domestic gas shortages this winter due to the conflict's disruption. The Trump administration is reportedly planning either a new military assault or tighter economic sanctions, while efforts to get neighbouring countries to enforce a blockade of Iran are struggling — most regional players are reluctant to get involved. Oil prices are sitting at around US$87 a barrel and could spike sharply if the conflict escalates around the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which a significant portion of the world's oil passes. For everyday Australians, this means higher fuel and energy costs are a real risk if things worsen.

stories.title: US midterms shake up Washington: Democrats push back on ICE raids, Republicans elect Jim Jordan as minority leader
stories.why_it_matters: The US midterm elections have reshuffled the political deck in Washington. Republicans suffered defeats and have elected hardliner Jim Jordan as the new House minority leader. Meanwhile, Democrats — emboldened by voter backlash against aggressive immigration enforcement — are pushing legislation to rein in Trump's ICE deportation raids. The White House fired back by warning Democrats not to investigate the Trump administration. The political gridlock in Washington adds to uncertainty for US markets and trade policy, which matters for anyone holding US shares.

stories.title: US House blocks impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
stories.why_it_matters: The US House of Representatives voted to block an attempt by Democrats to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth has been a controversial figure since his appointment, with critics questioning his suitability for the role. The failed impeachment bid — defeated along party lines — signals that Republicans retain enough unity to protect Trump's cabinet despite midterm losses. It keeps Hegseth in place as the US manages its ongoing military operations, including the Iran conflict.

stories.title: World's largest artificial reef created by sinking ocean liner SS United States
stories.why_it_matters: In a remarkable piece of history-meets-environment news, the SS United States — once the world's fastest ocean liner — was deliberately sunk off the US coast to create what is now the world's largest artificial reef. The ship, which held the transatlantic speed record, was scuttled after years of sitting derelict. Artificial reefs like this become thriving marine ecosystems within years, attracting fish, coral, and divers. It's a rare good-news story for ocean conservation.

stories.title: Major British supermarket chain in crisis talks over future
stories.why_it_matters: An unnamed major British supermarket chain is in emergency board meetings to discuss its options, with reports suggesting it is under serious financial pressure. The UK retail sector has been squeezed by high interest rates, rising labour costs, and consumers trading down to discount rivals. While the specific chain hasn't been confirmed in public reporting, any collapse of a major UK grocer would affect tens of thousands of workers and suppliers. Worth watching if you have any exposure to UK retail or broader European consumer stocks.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 was essentially flat today, dipping just 0.07% to 9,146 points as local investors digested a mixed global picture. Last night in the US, it was a strong night — the S&P 500 jumped 1.31% and the NASDAQ surged 1.6%, boosted by tech stocks including Google. Gold slipped 0.87% to US$3,965 as some risk-on appetite returned. Oil was steady at US$86.92. The Aussie dollar weakened slightly to US$0.6827.

indicators.note: Flat session locally — cautious mood with global uncertainties.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Strong night in the US last night, led by tech.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech rallied hard last night — Google was a standout.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil steady despite Iran war tensions and stalled ceasefire talks.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold eased slightly as risk appetite returned to markets last night.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar slipped — a weaker AUD complicates the RBA's inflation fight but boosts AUD value of your US holdings.

politics.summary: PM Albanese is at COP31 defending Australia's climate credentials, while back home there's political noise around his Treasurer and the RBA faces criticism over its aggressive rate-hiking cycle. Australia is also set to become the first country with mandatory AI safety laws.

stories.title: Albanese at COP31: Defends Australia as a climate leader amid calls for more action
stories.why_it_matters: Prime Minister Albanese is representing Australia at COP31 (the UN climate summit) and is pushing back against international pressure to do more. He's defending Australia's current emissions reduction targets while facing criticism from other nations and climate advocates that the country isn't moving fast enough. Former PM Malcolm Turnbull has weighed in, backing means-testing of EV and home battery subsidies — arguing taxpayer money for clean energy should go to those who need it most, not wealthy households who'd buy EVs anyway. This debate will shape Australia's energy and cost-of-living policies heading into the next budget.

stories.title: Treasurer under pressure as PM publicly backs him amid replacement rumours
stories.why_it_matters: While Albanese is abroad at COP31, there are rumours swirling in Canberra about the future of his Treasurer. Albanese publicly backed his Treasurer today before departing, but the fact he felt the need to do so publicly suggests the speculation is serious enough to address. Political instability in economic leadership can unsettle business confidence and markets, particularly when big decisions like a mid-year budget update are approaching.

stories.title: RBA under fire: Australia hiked rates faster than any other advanced economy
stories.source: Switzer Daily / The Guardian / Ticker News
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis published today reveals that Australia's Reserve Bank hiked interest rates faster and harder than any other advanced economy this year. Critics are now openly asking whether the RBA went too far — one commentator bluntly accused the bank of 'trying to achieve full employment by increasing unemployment,' meaning rate hikes slow the economy and cost jobs. The good news: there are growing signals that rate hikes are over, which would be a relief for mortgage holders. However, the AFR warns that a weakening Aussie dollar is now threatening to reignite inflation — potentially forcing the RBA's hand again.

stories.title: Australia to impose world-first mandatory AI safety rules; tech bosses face criminal charges
stories.why_it_matters: Australia is set to become the first country in the world to impose mandatory safety regulations on AI companies. The push was triggered in part by a review into a major Medicare data hack that exposed millions of Australians' health records. Under the proposed laws, tech executives could face criminal charges if their AI systems cause serious harm and they failed to take reasonable precautions. It's a significant move that will affect how global AI companies operate in Australia — and it comes as a new poll shows most Australians actually want tougher AI rules.

ai.summary: AI regulation is dominating the local conversation today, with Australia moving toward world-first mandatory safety laws. Meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI both launched new features competing directly with Microsoft and Google, and the ANZ bank CEO is warning of a global jobs crisis without better AI guardrails.

stories.title: Australia to become first country with mandatory AI safety laws — and bosses could face jail
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government is pushing ahead with mandatory AI safety regulations — a world first. Tech executives whose AI systems cause serious harm could face criminal charges if they're found to have ignored reasonable precautions. The move was partly driven by a government review into the Medicare data breach. Debate is now raging about whether Australia is focused on the right risks — some argue the rules target headline-grabbing dangers while missing subtler, more likely harms like biased decision-making in housing or employment.

stories.title: Anthropic and OpenAI launch new features going head-to-head with Microsoft and Google
stories.why_it_matters: Both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT) launched significant new features this week that directly compete with tools already offered by Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. The AI arms race is accelerating — these companies are now all chasing the same enterprise and consumer customers. For Microsoft and Google shareholders, this means competition is intensifying, though both giants have deep integration advantages (Office, Search) that newcomers can't easily replicate.

stories.title: ANZ CEO warns of global jobs crisis if AI goes unregulated
stories.why_it_matters: ANZ Bank CEO Nuno Matos spoke at a Bloomberg summit today, warning that without proper global AI regulations, the world is heading for a significant jobs crisis. He argued that AI is advancing faster than governments and businesses can adapt, and without guardrails, entire industries could face rapid displacement of workers with no safety net in place. It's a notable intervention from a major Australian banking figure — and adds weight to the push for the new Australian AI laws.

stories.title: Students organise nationwide rallies against AI
stories.why_it_matters: Student groups around Australia are organising nationwide protests against artificial intelligence, particularly its use in education, creative industries, and job recruitment. The rallies reflect growing community anxiety about AI replacing human work and being used to make high-stakes decisions (like university admissions) without transparency. It's a sign that the politics of AI regulation will only intensify — and that any company seen as reckless with AI faces real reputational risk.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — the Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Rugby League World Cup fever is building with the Australia vs New Zealand final looming, while the AFL enters its off-season with the draft and trade period dominating headlines. Roger Federer claimed a record eighth Wimbledon title.

stories.title: NRL Grand Final: Roosters beat Knights 19-18 in a one-point thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters claimed the 2026 NRL premiership with a heart-stopping 19-18 victory over the Newcastle Knights at Accor Stadium on Sunday night. It doesn't get closer than this — one point separating the teams at full time. It was a fitting end to the season after both clubs battled through the finals series. Roosters fans on the Gold Coast will be celebrating; Knights fans will be hurting for a while.

stories.title: RLWC 2026 Final: Australia vs New Zealand — teams and preview
stories.why_it_matters: The Rugby League World Cup 2026 is coming down to a Trans-Tasman final between Australia and New Zealand — the classic RLWC matchup. Team lists have been confirmed and previews are out ahead of what promises to be a ferocious contest. Australia will be favourites on home soil, but the Kiwis have the talent to cause an upset. A must-watch for any league fan.

stories.title: NRL to introduce Wildcard Round — shock announcement
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL has announced a Wildcard Round will be introduced to the competition — a significant structural change that would give additional clubs a second chance to qualify for the finals. Details are still emerging, but it could reshape the final weeks of the regular season and the finals format. Teams that miss the top eight would potentially get one more shot. Big news for every club's end-of-season calculations.

stories.title: Roger Federer wins record eighth Wimbledon title
stories.why_it_matters: Roger Federer claimed a record-breaking eighth Wimbledon title, defeating Marin Cilic in what was described as a dominant performance. The win surpasses his own all-time record at the All England Club and cements his status as arguably the greatest grass-court player in history. Jannik Sinner, meanwhile, has revealed an Australian Open target after recovering from a knee injury — giving fans something to look forward to heading into the summer Grand Slam season.

stories.title: AFL Draft: Lions eyeing major move, Bombers' bizarre scenario explained
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL off-season is heating up with the draft order now finalised. The Brisbane Lions are reportedly chasing a significant draft trade to secure a highly rated young talent. Meanwhile, the Essendon Bombers are caught in a complicated draft scenario — Fox Sports has laid out the unusual circumstances that could affect their pick positions. Richmond has also confirmed coaching changes as the Tigers rebuild after a tough season. The off-season chess match is well underway.
